data.title: Reporting an archaeological find pays off – the finder’s reward is yours
data.excerpt: Every archaeological find is, as part of the cultural heritage, the property of the Slovak Republic – but the finder who reports one properly is entitled to a reward of up to 100 % of its value. The article explains what counts as an archaeological find, how and to whom it has to be reported, why it must be left at the find spot, and how much has been paid out for individual finds.
data.metaTitle: Reporting an archaeological find pays off: the finder’s reward
data.metaDescription: Archaeological finds in Slovakia belong to the state, yet a finder who reports one properly is entitled to a reward of up to 100 % of the find’s value.

children.text: Every archaeological find is, as part of the cultural heritage, the property of the Slovak Republic. State ownership of archaeological finds exists in most countries of the world.

Not only archaeologists but also „ordinary“ citizens come across the „sherds“ of our ancestors by chance during building and agricultural work or on a trip into the countryside. Unfortunately, many finds are deliberately concealed, and in doing so, besides impoverishing the cultural heritage and committing an administrative offence (a fine of up to €400,000) or a criminal offence (up to 10 years in prison), the finder also deprives himself of the entitlement to the finder’s reward, which is in essence a reward for honesty and for the correct procedure. A chance find, of course, cannot be made by deliberate searching with a metal detector. 
 
 A finder’s reward of up to 100 % of the value of the find has been paid by the Monuments Board since 1 June 2009. Before that, a reward of 100 % was given only in the case of finds made of precious metals or of other valuable materials; in the other cases the reward amounted to a sum equal to 20 % of the value of the find. As a matter of interest, in the Czech Republic the finder’s reward is max. 10 % (max. 100 % of the value of the material in the case of precious metals), in Italy max. 25 %, in Romania max. 45 % and in Spain 50 % of the value of the find. A finder’s reward of more than 100 % is paid in Norway, Sweden and Finland.
What is an archaeological find?

children.text: Every state has its own definition of a find. The Slovak statutory definition is as follows: „An archaeological find is a movable thing which is evidence of human life and activity from the earliest times up to the year 1918 and which as a rule has been found, or is located, in the ground, on its surface or under water. An archaeological find is also a weapon, ammunition, cartridges, a part of a uniform, military equipment or other military material which has been found in the ground, on its surface or under water and dates from before the year 1946.“
A find is therefore a discarded, lost, abandoned or hidden artefact which got (mainly) into the ground before the year 1919 and, in the case of military artefacts, before 1946.

Human skeletal remains outside functioning cemeteries are finds as well. It still happens that only the police are called out to skeletal remains, and even though they establish on the spot that the remains got into the ground before 1919, or 1946 respectively, they do not report this to the Regional Monuments Board. The police do not know the archaeological methods of documenting and investigating a find spot, and so we needlessly lose important information.
How and to whom should an archaeological find be reported?

You must report a chance find to the competent Regional Monuments Board, either directly or through the municipality, at the latest on the second working day. I do not recommend reporting a find through the municipality, since many municipalities do not know how to proceed correctly after a find has been reported. The ideal thing is to contact the competent Regional Monuments Board by email (contacts) and by telephone at the same time (contacts). The regional archaeologists spend a great deal of time out of the office, so if you cannot get through to them, call the registry office (contacts), which will give you their mobile telephone number, or they will call you back as soon as possible. You must also leave the find unchanged until it has been inspected by the Regional Monuments Board (KPÚ) or by a person authorised by it (an archaeologist licensed to carry out archaeological excavations).

It may happen to you that you find finds (basically pottery sherds) at a site already known to archaeologists and that, once you have reported them, the archaeologist tells you there is no reason to lift them. If the site is not threatened with destruction (for example by building work), or if you did not find the finds in a disturbed archaeological feature, then from a professional point of view, without a proper excavation, there is no reason to collect all the sherds from the surface of the site, because these come to the surface (for example through ploughing) every year. Those who loot sites are mostly not interested in pottery sherds, since with few exceptions they cannot be turned into money.

Finds of weapons, ammunition and cartridges from the world wars, even though they are archaeological finds, have to be reported to the police. The police then inform the KPÚ and the Monuments Board of the place, type and calibre of such a find.
When does the entitlement to the finder’s reward arise?

Once the above conditions have been met (that the find was made by chance, that it was reported within the set time limit and that it was left in place), you are entitled to the finder’s reward, which will be paid to you, if you apply for it, after a report on the chance archaeological find and an expert valuation have been prepared. If you did not know the correct procedure and failed to keep the time limit for reporting, or did not leave the find in place, report it all the same without hesitation (even after years). Nobody has yet been punished for such a minor breach of the law, nor is it in the public interest.

It should also be stressed that most finds have a very small value (for example most sherds and coins). The silver coins from the hoard found in Bratislava – Devínska Nová Ves, for instance, have an average value of about €3 apiece. The great value of this hoard (€30,000) was created by the very large number of coins (10,268).
Why is it necessary to leave an archaeological find at the find spot?

This is important in order to verify the circumstances of the find, to document the find spot and, where appropriate, to complete the investigation of the find. For example, after 1,732 coins from the hoard at Šurany had been handed over, another 24 coins were subsequently traced at the find spot, and at Kostolné Kračany, after 312 coins and several sherds of the vessel in which the hoard had been placed had been handed over, another 18 coins and further sherds of the vessel were found at the find spot and in the earth from the excavation at the find spot.

If you are afraid that the find may be damaged, destroyed or stolen before the archaeologist arrives, inform him of this and take photographs or video documentation of the find at the spot, including points in the surroundings that can be identified afterwards (for example a house, a tree, a rock). If necessary, guard the find until the archaeologist arrives. The finder has the right to reimbursement of the expenses connected with reporting and protecting (guarding) the find.
What happens if you report an archaeological find or hand it over to a museum or an archaeological institute?

Since monuments boards have existed in Slovakia only since 2002, many people still intuitively hand finds over to museums and to the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences, but these cannot pay out the finder’s reward, they have no competence to investigate a find on a building site if the landowner or the developer does not wish it, and many museums do not employ an archaeologist, or at least not an archaeologist licensed to carry out archaeological excavations.

Museums and the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences are obliged to inform the competent KPÚ once a chance find has been reported to them or accepted by them, but mostly they do not do so, and as a result the KPÚ does not learn, for example, of a new archaeological site to which it would pay increased attention if it were threatened by building activity (it would, for instance, order a rescue excavation there).

Most of the finds that reach the Monuments Board after being reported are in time transferred to museums, so the KPÚ/the Monuments Board is only an „administrative“ stop before the artefact is finally deposited or displayed in a museum.
Reporting the concealment of an archaeological find

If you know of the deliberate concealment of a find which the finder does not want to hand over, or if you know of the destruction of a find, please report it to the Monuments Board, to the public prosecutor’s office or to the police, best of all to two of these bodies at the same time, so that supervision of the investigation of your report is ensured. It may be possible to save the find, or at least part of it, after the event, or at any rate to obtain information that will help in protecting the archaeological heritage.
